title: Novaya Gazeta v Voronezhe v. Russia
facts:
The applicant is the Editorial Board of the Novaya Gazeta v Voronezhe newspaper, a limited liability company registered in Voronezh. On 2 April 2002 the newspaper published an article by Mr E.P. entitled "Atomic Mayor". It concerned abuses and irregularities allegedly committed by Mr S., the mayor of Novovoronezh, and other municipal officials, including Mr B., a deputy head of administration and director of the economy and finance department, and Mr P., chairman of the education committee. It also mentioned private parties supplying goods or services to the municipal authorities, including Mr F., a local businessman who did renovation work for State-funded institutions. The article quoted extensively from the Report on the Composite Audit of the Novovoronezh Town Administration, carried out by the Audit Department of the Ministry of Finance for the Voronezh Region from 13 November to 27 December 2001.

On 8 May 2002 Mr S., Mr B., Mr P. and Mr F. sued the applicant for defamation, claiming that the following extracts were untrue and damaging:
"... In autumn 2001 a group of campaigners in Novovoronezh collected signatures for a vote of no confidence in Vladimir S. They collected nearly three thousand signatures ..." [paragraph 4]
"... For a long time the Novovoronezh town administration failed to transfer payments to the compulsory medical insurance fund. In the mayor's opinion, these transfers were not mandatory, but a commercial court decided otherwise. Thanks to S., in 2002 the town budget will lose a further twenty million [roubles] ..." [21]
"... Mayor S. still adheres to the ideas of Socialism and Communism; not only once did he enter the ranks of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation ... occasionally he left its ranks ..." [23]
"... [In addition to the budget, Novovoronezh has an off-budget fund. And a substantial one.] One would only wonder at the way the mayor and his faithful companion, comrade B., the head of the economy and finance department doubling as executive director of all funds, handled its assets ... Thus, thanks to the efforts of two prominent economists, the town lost an amount comparable to nearly one half of the annual budget ..." [34, 47]
"The chairman of the education committee of the Novovoronezh administration, Mr P., did not produce any documents showing that these students came from needy or large families as he claimed ... What kind of needy families were these if even Mr P., the chairman of the education committee, does not know them?" [57, 58]
"Inquisitive readers would ask: why did Mr B. care so much about the military unit in the village of Boevo and the regional psychiatric hospital (let's recall the charitable contribution of 300,000 roubles made to the hospital)? And they would start looking for an answer. Is it not in military unit no. 51205 that the son of the aforementioned official is doing his military service? Is it not in the regional psychiatric hospital that a relation or a namesake of Mr B. has just undergone a medical examination in order to escape punishment for a serious criminal offence? ... [67-69] And what about the honest Mayor S.? He does not know, perhaps, about the tricks of his deputy? On the contrary. He does know and he even personally signs payment orders for the transfer of money to the State enterprise 'Voronezh regional clinical psychiatric hospital'..." [71, 72]
"The thing is that the notion of competitions (tenders) for the provision of services for State-funded organisations ceased to exist in the town long ago. If our fair and Communist-minded mayor S. liked Mr P. (they have done much business together), he could have as much work as he liked. He could supply computers at 150,000 roubles a piece and feed children in kindergartens at inflated prices ..." [87]
"... During the audit an estimate of the repair work actually performed in the town stadium was made up. The cost of the actual work done amounted to nearly 500,000 roubles. So, Mr S. and Mr F., where have the remaining 1,300,000 roubles gone? ..." [93]

On 10 and 11 September 2002 the Sovetskiy District Court of Voronezh took evidence. The plaintiffs produced commercial court judgments under which RUB 26,927 had been recovered from the municipal authorities in respect of medical insurance payments. Mr S. produced a document showing he had been a Communist Party member since 1995 and had never relinquished membership. The applicant had only ordinary (uncertified) copies of the audit report and of the report of 22 November 2001 on the verification of work at the stadium and shooting gallery; as ordinary copies had no evidentiary value, it asked the court to obtain the originals. The court refused because the applicant had not shown it had tried to obtain them itself. Throughout October 2002 the applicant unsuccessfully sought the originals from the regional Audit Department, the town department of the interior and the regional and town prosecutors' offices, and renewed its request for a court injunction. On 30 October 2002 the trial court refused the request without stating reasons in the judgment. Mr S. withdrew his claim regarding paragraph 4.

The same day the trial court found all contested extracts untrue and damaging. It stated: "In such cases, pursuant to Article 152 of the Russian Civil Code, the defendant shall prove the truthfulness of the information disseminated, whilst the plaintiff is only required to show that the defendant disseminated the information. Not only assertions, but also conjectures shall be amenable to proof. Damaging conjectures which are shown to have been unfounded in a court hearing will give rise to an apology. Reliance on rumours, hearsay, opinions of anonymous experts, competent sources, etc. as the basis for the damaging information shall not relieve the defendant from the obligation to show its truthfulness..." It held that paragraphs 93-94 implied embezzlement by Mr S. and Mr F., noting the audit report assessed the total cost of work at RUB 1,850,000 and no proof of embezzlement had been adduced. As to Mr S., it held the statement that the town would lose 20 million thanks to the mayor was incorrect because the payments were mandatory and recovered by court order in the same amount; the 'discontinuous' party membership claim was untrue; paragraph 47 wrongly blamed Mr S. and Mr B. since the structure of off-budget funds was regulated by federal government decision; and paragraph 87 conveyed that dishonest men under the mayor's patronage profited from kindergartens without evidence. As to Mr B., the defendants had failed to prove he was executive director of 'all funds', that a relation, especially a criminal, had hidden or been treated in the psychiatric hospital, or that he and Mr S. misspent the budget. It accepted that the allegations about Mr P.'s involvement in abuses in student selection were insulting. It stated: "Thus, the court has concluded that the plaintiffs' claims are well-founded because the author and the editors tolerated the publication of an article that contained insulting and untrue statements... without bothering to check all the relevant facts. In accordance with the law... evidence should have been collected before the information was published and it is inappropriate to start collecting evidence after the article was published... Moreover, the plaintiffs have produced before the court a reply from the Novovoronezh prosecutor's office and a decision of the Novovoronezh police department refusing criminal prosecution in connection with the audit of certain financial matters in the education committee of Novovoronezh in 2000-2001." It ordered the applicant to pay RUB 10,000 to Mr S. and RUB 5,000 each to Mr B., Mr P. and Mr F. (RUB 25,000 total) and to publish an apology.

On 8 January 2003 the applicant appealed, arguing the article concerned a matter of public interest, the plaintiffs as public figures and State servants should tolerate more criticism, the article was largely founded on the audit report, the court had denied it an opportunity to prove facts by refusing to obtain the originals, and it had been ordered to refute value judgments. The appeal statement recounted that the trial court had considered the first document unnecessary because the file contained a police decision to institute a criminal investigation into the facts in the audit report, and the second unnecessary because the police had forwarded it to the prosecutor's office. On 6 February 2003 the Voronezh Regional Court upheld the judgment, finding the value-judgment argument unsubstantiated and stating: "The dissemination of the information that the plaintiffs seek to refute was proven before the [trial] court and has not been disputed by the respondent. Accordingly the newspaper was obliged to submit evidence before the [trial] court to prove the truthfulness of the information in question. However, no such evidence was presented before the [trial] court."

On 20 June 2003 the applicant paid RUB 25,000 to the bailiffs' service and published an apology in the 11-17 July 2003 issue retracting the article. Under Article 152 of the Civil Code and Resolution no. 11 of the Plenary Supreme Court (1992, as amended 1995), the plaintiff had to prove dissemination and the defendant had to prove the truth of the disseminated 'information' (svedeniya).
applicantSubmissions: The disputed statements in the article were supported by the stadium report and the audit report issued by the Audit Department of the Ministry of Finance for the Voronezh Region.

It had been impossible to use the reports as evidence because the author had only ordinary copies, not originals or certified copies, and the domestic courts refused to request the originals or certified copies.

The domestic courts' refusal to request the originals or certified copies of the reports had a chilling effect on journalists in possession of ordinary copies of official documents capable of disclosing a matter of public interest.
The refusal to open criminal proceedings concerning the facts described in the reports could not, in itself, render the information contained in them false.
The requirement to prove the truth of a value judgment is not compatible with freedom of expression, yet the courts required the applicant to prove value judgments.

The trial court's reasoning for refusing to request certified copies of the documents had been communicated to counsel only via unofficial channels; the trial minutes contained no reference to that reasoning, which is why counsel referred to it in the appeal statement.
governmentSubmissions: The disputed statements were statements of fact and not value judgments.

The domestic courts independently assessed the evidence before them and decided on its relevance; the trial court had sufficient evidence submitted by the parties to decide the civil dispute without using other evidence.
The trial court's refusal to request the originals of the audit and stadium reports was well-reasoned and the applicant had been duly notified of the reasons.

The applicant could have complained to a court about the prosecutor's office's failure to provide the originals, but did not do so; and if the reasons were not recorded in the trial minutes, it could have requested modification of the minutes under domestic law.
The judgment was based on Article 152 of the Civil Code because the applicant failed to prove the veracity of the statements made in the article.
The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of others.

The interference was necessary in a democratic society because the article suggested that the plaintiffs had committed illegal acts, creating a pressing need to protect them and prevent careless use of such serious allegations.
